question: A 4-year-old girl presents with a 3-week history of fever, pallor, fatigue, and easy bruising. Examination reveals generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone tenderness on palpation. CBC shows Hb 6.1 g/dL, WBC 45 × 10⁹/L with blasts, and platelets 22 × 10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well child. Pancytopenia with blasts, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone tenderness excludes ITP — these features indicate bone marrow infiltration.

Correct. ALL is the most common childhood malignancy (~30% of all paediatric cancers). The triad of bone-marrow-failure features (anaemia + thrombocytopenia + neutropenia/infection), peripheral blasts, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and bone tenderness from marrow infiltration are characteristic.
Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia but the bone marrow is hypocellular with fatty replacement — there are no blasts. It does not cause hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.

EBV causes infectious mononucleosis with atypical lymphocytes, not blasts. The Hb and platelet counts are typically preserved, and the degree of splenomegaly with bone tenderness is not characteristic of EBV.

overallFeedback.feedback: This presentation — pancytopenia with blasts, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and bone tenderness — is classic ALL. ALL is the most common childhood malignancy and requires urgent bone marrow confirmation.

Correct! The ALL triad: anaemia + thrombocytopenia + neutropenia/infection, PLUS hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, and blasts. Confirm with bone marrow aspiration (≥25% lymphoblasts) and immunophenotyping.
